It is a meadow. The grass is tall and the soil is soft. I see the foxes there. They run and dig. I hear them. I hear the wind in the grass. I hear the mice. I hear the night.

From the hollow in the ash by the lane. I fly out over the lane, past the barn, over the stream and the meadow. I hunt voles, shrews, beetles and mice. I do not see the lane from the air, only the stream and the meadow. I land in the oak on the other side of the stream. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

From the oak by the stream. The stream is wide, so I go up the hill to the top of the wood. I fly in the wind, not the air. I see the light fade and the voles come out.

From the oak at the end of the lane. I wait for the light to fade. The first beetles come up in the field. I fly out in a straight line, a silent arrow, and catch them in the air. The lane is safe. I always return to the oak.

I fly out from the oak, circling the meadow and the stream. I listen for the rustle of voles in the grass, the splash of a frog in the water, or the flutter of a mouse in the hedgerow. From the oak. I call and listen. The voles come out. I fly low and fast. I catch them in the ivy. The wood is full of them. I fly east, west, north, south. I hunt the meadow and the stream. I call to the mate. I fly back. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly from the oak, over the meadow, past the stream, and up the lane. I circle the village, looking for movement in the shadows. I search the hedgerows, the fence posts, the roof tops. From the oak. I wait in the hollow until the light fades. Then I drop down into the meadow and hunt. I go for voles, shrews, mice. I do not go far. The meadow is close. I call to the others as I fly. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
From the oak, the same one I have nested in. I fly out into the meadow, the whole of it, and the stream. I turn in the wind, I listen, I wait.

From the hollow. I call hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. My mate answers ke-wick. Then I fly. I fly low, over the grass, over the stream. I hunt voles and mice. I find them in the meadow, in the field. I strike, I catch, I eat. I leave the rest. I fly back to the hollow. I am full.

A road. It runs through the meadow on the other side of the stream. I have not crossed it. I have heard the growl of a fox, and the screech of a cat. The road is wide and lit by lamps at night. I do not like it. I have seen no owls on it.
The meadow beyond the edge. It is all grass and no cover, and the road runs through it. I hear the car engines and the dogs. The meadow is not safe. I do not go there.

A road. A stream. A field. A lane. A lane with lights. A lane with voices. A lane with dogs. I do not go beyond the edge. I do not need to. The wood is my world. The lane is not. I hear the dogs. I hear the voices. I hear the lights. I do not answer. I do not go. I am here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The meadow. The stream. The road. The lights. The dogs. The men with loud voices and bright things. Beyond the edge of the wood, the world is different. There is no hollow, no silence, no owl. The meadow beyond the edge of the wood is where the voles run. I can hear them under the grass, squeaking and scurrying. The wind carries the smell of damp earth and the distant call of a barn owl. A road, and a stream, and the village. The road is quiet at night, but the lights bother me. The stream is cold and sings. The village is far, with many lights and voices. I do not go there. I stay in my wood, where the hoot is familiar and the meadow is soft underfoot.

The edge of my wood is the road. It runs straight, black, and cold. I hear it at night, the cars going fast, the dogs barking. Beyond the road is the meadow, then the stream, then the valley. A meadow, dry and brown. A stream, cold and fast. A road, wide and bright. People move there, in cars and in lights. They do not know the wood. They do not hear the owls. They do not see the mice. A road, and beyond that a meadow, and beyond that the river. I do not go there. The road is too loud with humans, and the meadow is too open. I stay in the wood.

Beyond the edge is the meadow, and beyond that the stream, and beyond that the lane. The lane is where the lights go on at night, and the cars go by. I do not go there.
